historyReviewBoundary: All 115 histories have author source checks. Final independent review covered metadata and numerical checks for all 115 classes, 12 deeper class targets and source-gap samples in seven classes. It did not independently verify every passage of every cited source.

history.name: Peripheral local-anesthetic antitussives

starting.description: Airway local anesthetics' cough-suppressing effects and experimental links between lung inflation and cough directed research toward an agent that would anesthetize pulmonary-distention-sensitive vagal fibers, according to contemporary clinical authors and a later review.

inspiration.description: Observed suppression of cough during local anesthesia and experimental relationships between inspiratory lung distention and cough intensity.

steps.description: Prior clinical effects of local anesthetics and experimental respiratory physiology directed research toward a peripheral antitussive, according to contemporary clinical authors and a later review.

Separately, a 1955 Matter patent described preparation of a p-butylaminobenzoate polyethoxy ester and pharmacological properties of the broader ester group. The patent does not document a cough rationale or establish whether this particular preparation followed the physiological observations.
Bucher investigated benzonatate's effects on lung stretch receptors, according to the review; 1958 clinical investigators tested Tessalon against induced cough and in patients.

design.description: Matter described preparing polyethoxy esters including the p-butylaminobenzoate member; the 1958 clinicians described polyethylene glycol replacing a diethylaminoethanol residue. Neither source establishes why the chemist first selected this exact structure for cough.

circumstances.description: The contemporary clinical report describes research directed toward selective anesthesia of pulmonary-distention-sensitive vagal fibers. It does not specify whether the first observation of the compound's antitussive effect was unexpected.

limits: The starting rationale for antitussive use is described by contemporary clinical researchers and a later review, not the chemical inventor; the class boundary excludes other antitussive lineages.
An earlier patent's priority does not date the particular compound example or establish why the chemical was first synthesized.
The peripheral target was a stated development rationale, not definitive proof of a unique clinical mechanism; the 1969 review recounts a competing central interpretation (E8).
conflicts: The 1969 review reports peripheral effects but notes that Sell, Lindner, and Jahn 1958 interpreted benzonatate's antitussive action as mainly central; the doses needed for consistent effects in those experiments were toxic, according to the review (E8). This mechanism dispute does not contradict the documented historical starting rationale.

In the 1958 induced-cough report, the authors describe subject 4 as unaltered, whereas their Table I lists 18 efforts before and 16 after; their wording and displayed counts should not be conflated (E7).
gaps: Bucher and Jacot 1951 and Bucher 1956 were located by metadata but their original texts were not read; their findings are attributed to the reviews (S1, S4).
The Sell, Lindner, and Jahn 1958 mechanistic study (S7) was not read directly; its characterization is attributed to S4.
The chemist's motive for selecting the particular structure and the exact transition from ester chemistry to cough testing are not established by the patent or clinical report.

humanContributionInterpretation.summary: Reduced coughing with local airway anesthesia during bronchoscopy supplied a clinical rationale for benzonatate.
humanContributionInterpretation.scope: Cat physiology also contributed; the clinical clue does not establish the original synthesis motive.
